title: Rare Rain Brings Colorful Wildflowers to Chile’s Atacama Desert
summary:
Colorful wildflowers are blooming across Chile’s Atacama Desert after rare rain linked to this year’s exceptionally strong El Niño. The bloom, described in a report published on October 2, 2026, has spread across hillsides and plains in one of the driest places on Earth.

The rain has awakened millions of seeds and bulbs that can stay underground for years. These resting seeds and bulbs can begin growing when enough moisture arrives. Areas that usually have little visible plant life are now covered with purple, pink, white, red and yellow flowers.

In Chile, this event is known as “desierto florido,” which means “flowering desert.” Jorge Carabantes, head of the Protected Areas Department at Chile’s National Forest Corp., known as CONAF, told The Associated Press that the event includes more than 200 plant species. He described this desert flowering as unusual and different from blooms elsewhere in the world.

The Atacama typically receives just 0.6 inches, or 15 millimeters, of rain each year. Between July and August this year, several Chilean regions received record rainfall. Carabantes said some areas received more than 190 millimeters, with rainfall levels in some regions not seen since the 1950s. These figures describe rainfall in several Chilean regions, rather than a single measurement for the whole desert.

The flowers now cover about 6,560 square miles, or 17,000 square kilometers, of the Atacama. CONAF representatives told The Associated Press that this is the desert’s most extensive bloom since 1997.

Tourists and photographers have visited to see the bright flowers against the mountains. Photographs also show cacti among the wildflowers and purple blossoms stretching across the plains.

The display will not last all year. By the end of spring in the Southern Hemisphere, many flowers will disappear. They will leave behind seeds and bulbs that can wait underground for another period of unusually heavy rain.
why_it_matters: The event illustrates how unusual rainfall can awaken resting desert plants across a large area. The article also distinguishes regional rainfall measurements from a measurement for the entire desert.
